def: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones (or compounds that give these on hydrolysis) made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
points: Monosaccharides: simplest sugars, cannot be hydrolysed further, e.g. glucose, fructose.
Oligosaccharides: give 2-10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis; disaccharides (2 units) like sucrose, maltose, lactose are the common type.
Polysaccharides: give many monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, e.g. starch, cellulose, glycogen.
Carbohydrates are also classed as reducing sugars (reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent, have free -CHO or -C=O) and non-reducing sugars (sucrose).
They are the main energy source and structural material (cellulose) in living organisms.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Carbohydrates"] --> B["Monosaccharides"]
  A --> C["Oligosaccharides"]
  A --> D["Polysaccharides"]
  C --> E["Disaccharides like sucrose maltose lactose"]
  D --> F["Starch cellulose glycogen"]

example: Sucrose (table sugar) is a disaccharide of glucose + fructose; starch is a polysaccharide made of many glucose units.
tip: Write the three-level classification with one example each - a common 2-mark question.

def: Glucose is an aldohexose (six-carbon sugar with an aldehyde group) and fructose is a ketohexose (six-carbon sugar with a ketone group); both have the molecular formula C6H12O6.
points: Glucose open chain structure: CHO-(CHOH)4-CH2OH, with the aldehyde group at C1.
Fructose open chain structure: CH2OH-CO-(CHOH)3-CH2OH, with the ketone group at C2.
Both molecules exist mainly in a cyclic (ring) form in solution: glucose forms a six-membered pyranose ring, fructose forms a five-membered furanose ring.
Glucose gives Fehling's and Tollens' test positive (reducing sugar) because of the free aldehyde group.
Glucose and fructose are structural isomers of each other (same formula, different structure).

diagram.draw: Draw the open-chain zig-zag skeleton for glucose: CHO at top (C1), then four CHOH carbons (C2-C5) each with OH labelled, ending in CH2OH (C6). Below it draw fructose similarly but with C=O at C2 instead of CHO at C1, and CH2OH at C1.

example: Glucose + Fehling's solution on heating gives a brick-red precipitate of Cu2O, confirming the aldehyde group.
tip: Mention 'isomers of each other' and the aldehyde vs ketone difference - frequently asked distinguishing point.

def: Proteins are natural polymers of amino acids joined together by peptide bonds, essential for body structure and function.
points: Amino acids link by a peptide bond (-CO-NH-) formed between the -COOH of one acid and -NH2 of the next, releasing water.
Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.
Secondary structure: regular folding of the chain into alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds.
Tertiary structure: overall 3-D folding of the protein giving its biological shape.
Quaternary structure: arrangement of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits) together, as in haemoglobin.
Classified as fibrous (insoluble, structural, e.g. keratin, collagen) or globular (soluble, functional, e.g. enzymes, insulin).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Primary structure sequence"] --> B["Secondary structure helix or sheet"]
  B --> C["Tertiary structure 3D folding"]
  C --> D["Quaternary structure multiple chains"]

example: Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains held together - an example of quaternary structure.
tip: List all four structural levels in order with one keyword each for full marks.

def: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins, that speed up biochemical reactions in living cells without being consumed.
points: Enzymes are highly specific - each enzyme acts on a particular substrate only.
Active site: a specific region on the enzyme where the substrate binds.
Mechanism (lock and key model): substrate fits into the active site forming an enzyme-substrate complex, which breaks down to give products and free enzyme.
Enzyme activity is affected by temperature and pH; most work best at body temperature (37°C) and specific pH.
Enzymes lower the activation energy of the reaction, increasing reaction rate.
Example enzymes: amylase (breaks starch to maltose), pepsin (digests proteins in stomach).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Enzyme E"] --> B["Enzyme substrate complex ES"]
  C["Substrate S"] --> B
  B --> D["Product P"]
  B --> E["Free enzyme E"]

example: Amylase in saliva converts starch into maltose during digestion of food in the mouth.
tip: Draw the lock-and-key diagram and mention 'activation energy decreases' for full marks.

def: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts in the diet for normal growth and health, as the body cannot synthesise most of them.
points: Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K - stored in the body, dissolve in fats.
Water-soluble vitamins: B-complex and C - not stored, excess excreted in urine, needed regularly in diet.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness (xerophthalmia).
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums).
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency causes beriberi.
formula: No single formula - classification only: fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B, C)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Vitamins"] --> B["Fat soluble A D E K"]
  A --> C["Water soluble B complex and C"]
  B --> D["Deficiency night blindness rickets"]
  C --> E["Deficiency beriberi scurvy"]

example: A sailor on a long voyage without fresh fruits develops scurvy due to vitamin C deficiency.
tip: Make a table: vitamin name, source, deficiency disease - this table format scores full marks.

def: Nucleic acids are biopolymers made of nucleotide units that store and transmit genetic information in living cells.
points: Each nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogen base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose sugar and bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine; it is double-stranded (double helix).
RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose sugar and bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil (no thymine); it is usually single-stranded.
In DNA, base pairing follows the rule: adenine pairs with thymine, guanine pairs with cytosine, held by hydrogen bonds.
DNA carries hereditary information; RNA helps in protein synthesis.
formula: Nucleotide = nitrogen base + pentose sugar + phosphate group

diagram.draw: Draw two parallel curved lines representing the double helix backbone of DNA. Connect them with short horizontal rungs labelled 'A-T' and 'G-C' base pairs at intervals. Label one strand 'sugar-phosphate backbone' and the base pair rungs 'hydrogen bonds'.

example: In a DNA strand with sequence A-T-G-C, the complementary strand reads T-A-C-G by base pairing rules.
tip: State clearly the sugar and base difference between DNA and RNA - a frequently asked distinguishing question.
